title: Introduction to NLP
oneLiner: What it takes for a computer to work with human language, why that is surprisingly hard, and the first clean-up steps every language system uses.

what.html:
Natural language processing (NLP) is about getting computers to read, understand and write human language: search engines, translators, spam filters, voice assistants and chatbots all use it. Language works in layers (word parts, words, grammar, meaning, the wider conversation, the situation), and a system has to handle all of them.

Everyday versionReading a friend's message "can u grab milk?" involves spelling ("u" = you), grammar, meaning, and context: it's a request, not a question about whether you're able to.

why.html:
• Most human knowledge is written down as text.
  • Language is ambiguous everywhere, so naive rules break.
  • Every modern language system still starts with these basic steps.

how.title: What NLP covers
how.html: Understanding and generating language, borrowing from linguistics, psychology and statistics. Used in predictive text, grammar checkers, search, translation, sentiment analysis, question answering and summarisation.

how.title: Layers of language
how.html: Word parts ("fire" + "house") → words → grammar → literal meaning → links between sentences ("she", "it") → meaning in the situation ("close the window" is a request).

how.title: Reading vs writing
how.html: Understanding (NLU) analyses what was said. Generation (NLG) decides what to say and then how to phrase it.

how.title: Ambiguity everywhere
how.html: "I saw bats" (animals or sports gear?). "I saw the man with the telescope" (who has it?). "Teacher strikes idle kids" (two completely different stories). Picking the right meaning needs knowledge, not just grammar.

how.title: More hard bits
how.html: Slang ("gm"), idioms ("dark horse"), names that look like phrases ("A Bug's Life"), and background knowledge: "Mary and Sue are sisters" vs "Mary and Sue are mothers".

how.title: Cleaning up text
how.html: Split into sentences (careful: "Dr." and "3.14" don't end sentences), split sentences into tokens, and sometimes drop very common words like "the" and "is".

how.title: Stems vs lemmas
how.html: Stemming chops endings ("studies" → "studi", not a real word). Lemmatisation finds the dictionary form ("studies" → "study", "better" → "good").

how.title: Grammar rules and trees
how.html: A small set of rules (sentence = noun phrase + verb phrase, …) builds a tree for a sentence. "Rice flies like sand" gets two trees: insects called rice flies, or rice flying like sand.

how.title: Measuring success
how.html: Count hits and misses and compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1. If almost everything is "not spam", a system that never flags spam still looks 95% accurate, so pick the right metric.

demo.html: Type any text and see it cut into sentences and tokens, stripped of stop words, and reduced to stems and lemmas.

example.html:
Three ways a sentence can fail. "Green frogs have large noses" is grammatical and meaningful, just odd. "Green ideas have large noses" is grammatical but meaningless (ideas aren't green). "Large have green ideas nose" isn't even grammatical. Getting the grammar right is necessary but not enough.

Supplementary Modern models use "subword" tokens, so a rare word like "unbelievably" may become pieces such as "un", "believ", "ably".

misunderstandings: Grammar alone is enough to understand language.
Meaning, discourse and context matter too.
A full stop always ends a sentence.
Abbreviations and decimals break that rule.
Stemming and lemmatisation are the same.
Stems can be non-words; lemmas are dictionary forms.
High accuracy means a good system.
Not on imbalanced data; check precision and recall.
takeaways: NLP analyses, understands and generates human language.
Levels: morphology → lexical → syntax → semantics → discourse → pragmatics.
Ambiguity (lexical, structural) is the core difficulty.
Pipeline: segmentation, tokenisation, stop words, stemming/lemmatisation.
CFGs make structural ambiguity explicit; evaluate with fitting metrics.
thirty: NLP makes computers analyse, understand and generate human language, drawing on AI, linguistics and statistics, and powers search, translation, assistants and more. Language is analysed in layers from morphology through lexical, syntactic, semantic and discourse analysis to pragmatics; a sentence can pass low levels and fail higher ones. NLU analyses input; NLG plans and realises output. Ambiguity at every level (lexical: 'bats'; structural: 'the man with the telescope') plus idioms, non-standard text, segmentation and world knowledge make it hard. Preprocessing segments sentences, tokenises, removes stop words, and stems (crude, fast) or lemmatises (dictionary-based). Context-free grammars (rules plus lexicon) generate parse trees and expose structural ambiguity ('rice flies like sand' has two parses). Systems are evaluated with task-appropriate metrics such as precision, recall and F1 on representative test sets, using toolkits like NLTK, spaCy and Gensim.

check.q: 'Colourless green ideas sleep furiously' fails at which level?
'I saw the man with the telescope' is an example of…
